title: Nobody Adopted Your Recommendation
author: Andrea Chiarelli
summary: Chiarelli opens with a familiar scene: a polished, well-evidenced recommendation is nodded at and dropped, while a rougher version of the same idea energises the room twenty minutes later. Her argument is that whether advice gets adopted is decided before anyone speaks, through trust and credibility accumulated over months. She makes the case through two composite stories. Maria, a researcher with no formal say in strategy, is invited into planning because she was consistently useful to other teams. Wei, a policy adviser, wins adoption by raising a serious flaw privately with his director beforehand and by building a track record of being right and honest about being wrong. The piece concludes that analytical rigour is necessary but insufficient, and that the relational side of influence is rarely taught. The closing section promotes the author's paid playbook, but the body stands on its own as a practical account of how influence is built.
points: Relationships built at the moment you need something are too late; trust has to be deposited in advance by being useful to other people's problems.
Credibility is a reputation across many pieces of work, so treat each recommendation as a chapter in a longer story about whether your judgement can be relied on.
Raising a flaw privately before the meeting, with alternatives in hand, lets a senior person adapt without being cornered in public.
Admitting openly when you were wrong is part of what makes your judgement worth trusting.
Analytical and technical skill get you hired but do not by themselves make your work land; influence has to be practised deliberately.
quotes: Most people have watched this happen. The difference between the person who gets heard and the person who doesn’t is usually about things that happened before they opened their mouth.

And Maria was already the person who came to mind. They didn’t have to go looking. She was already in their peripheral vision, because she’d spent months making herself useful to other people’s problems rather than just delivering against her own.
Maria had been depositing trust for months without making a withdrawal, and when the moment came, the relationship was already there.

The difference was that they treated each recommendation as a standalone piece of analysis, delivered and forgotten. Wei treated each one as a chapter in a longer story about whether his judgement could be relied on.

The lesson here is that credibility isn’t something you can assert or attach to a single piece of work. It’s a reputation, built over time, and the people who have it are the ones who think about what their track record says about them as much as what their current paper says about the problem.

The skills that get you hired (analytical rigour, technical expertise, clear writing) are necessary but insufficient. They’ll make your work good, but they won’t make it land. The part that determines whether anyone acts on what you’ve produced is rarely assessed, and almost never developed deliberately.
